---
order: 3
title: "Symmetric MultiZenoTravel"
subtitle: "Proposition I: the Pareto front is reached with exactly 2t − p central cities"
css: ../styles/paper.css
---

The method to find the Pareto Front of any general MultiZenoTravel instance consists of three
steps. First, we provide an efficient algorithm to find the Pareto Front for any symmetric clique
MultiZenoTravel instance. Then, we show that for the non-symmetric version of the problem the
method still applies when flights between central cities are not shorter than a detour through
$C_I$ or $C_G$, provided waiting is accounted for, and that it does not otherwise. Last, we study
the transformation of any instance of the general MultiZenoTravel problem into a non-symmetric
clique version, and the cases in which it preserves the Pareto front. This section covers the
first step; it corresponds to §2 to §4 of the
[theory note](https://github.com/aquemy/ZenoSolver/blob/master/doc/theory/exact-front.md).

The following proposition is the cornerstone of the method to identify and construct the Pareto
Set of any instance:

::: {.statement}
**Proposition I**: Assume (S), and (AΔ) or (A1). Every point of the Pareto front is attained by a
plan where exactly $2t - p$ (possibly identical) central cities are used by a plane.
:::

Under (A1), Proposition I is {{< node "Theorem 4.7" >}} together with
{{< node "Corollary 4.8" >}}; under (AΔ), it is {{< node "Theorem 4.10" >}}, from which
{{< node "Corollary 4.12" >}} carries Corollary 4.8 over.

By Corollary II, no plan uses fewer than $2t - p$ central cities, so Proposition I reduces the
search to lists of $2t - p$ cities. It is a statement about the front: with landing costs of
zero, a Pareto-optimal plan may land more often. With one city of duration 1 and cost 0, $p = 3$
and $t = 5$, the front is $\{(0, 6)\}$, attained by planes landing 3, 3 and 1 times; the plane
landing once can add a pattern $\bar A$ and a pattern $A$ within its slack, and the resulting
plan, with 9 landings, still attains $(0, 6)$.

The goal of this section is to establish the proof of Proposition I for the Symmetric case. For
that purpose, we first describe which lists of $2t - p$ cities can be flown, and how fast. We then
show that every plan is dominated by one of them, first under the assumption (A1) of
[[QS15](index.qmd#ref-QS15)], then under the triangular inequality (AΔ). Precisely, with
$$M(X) = \min\Big\{\max_k \ell(X_k) : X_1, \dots, X_p \text{ an admissible partition of } X\Big\},$$
the front is the Pareto set of the pairs $(c(X), M(X))$ over the lists $X$ of $2t - p$ cities.

## Admissible partitions {#sec-admissible}

A list of $2t - p$ cities does not hold any information about which plane will land in a
particular city. Assign to each plane $k$ the cities $X_k$ in which it lands: when can the
partition $X_1, \dots, X_p$ be flown with simple patterns? By Lemma 2.1, a plane performs one
more $A$ than $\bar A$, so a plane that performs only those patterns lands an odd number of times.
A plane that lands an even number of times has to perform a pattern $B$ or $\bar B$, that is, to
leave a passenger in a central city for another plane, or to take one left there by another
plane. These hand-offs pair up at each city. Admissibility records exactly this bookkeeping,
modulo 2.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Definition 2.2" >}} **Admissible partition.** A *parity matrix* for $X_1, \dots, X_p$
is a matrix $h \in \{0, 1\}^{p \times n}$ such that

* (h1) $h_{k,i} = 1$ implies $X_k(i) \ge 1$;
* (h2) $\sum_i h_{k,i} \equiv |X_k| + 1 \pmod 2$ for every plane $k$;
* (h3) $\sum_k h_{k,i} \equiv 0 \pmod 2$ for every city $i$.

The partition is *admissible* if it has a parity matrix.
:::

Here $h_{k,i} = 1$ means that plane $k$ takes part in an odd number of hand-offs in city $i$.
(h2) asks a plane with an even group, an *even plane*, to do so in an odd number of cities, and
(h3) pairs the hand-offs of every city. An empty group would need an odd number of marked cities
in which it does not land, so admissible partitions have non-empty groups. The condition reads
more simply on a graph.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Lemma 2.4" >}} **Component form.** Let $H$ be the bipartite graph on planes and cities
with an edge between $k$ and $i$ whenever $X_k(i) \ge 1$. The partition is admissible if and only
if every connected component of $H$ contains an even number of even planes.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* A parity matrix is a set of edges of $H$ with odd degree exactly at the even planes, so
each component has an even number of them; conversely, such a set is built bottom-up in any
spanning forest of $H$ ({{< node "Lemma 2.4" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

On the [example instance](model.qmd#fig-plan), the groups $\{2, 3\}$ and $\{2, 3\}$ are
admissible: both planes are even, and they share cities. The groups $\{1, 1\}$ and $\{3, 3\}$ are
not: each plane is even, but they share no city, so each would have to hand a passenger to a plane
that never comes to its city. Two odd groups, such as $\{1\}$ and $\{1, 1, 1\}$, are always
admissible, and {{< node "Lemma 2.9" >}} shows that a partition with
$\sum_k |X_k| \equiv p \pmod 2$ is admissible as soon as some city belongs to every even group.

## (BB̄)-pairings and link forests {#sec-links}

A *($B\bar B$)-pairing* in city $i$ is a pattern $B$ of one plane and a pattern $\bar B$ of
another plane, both in $i$, carrying the same passenger: the first plane leaves it in $i$, the
second takes it to $C_G$. The parity matrix says in which cities the pairings are, but not between
which planes. A link forest says both.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Definition (link forest)" >}} A *link forest* for $X_1, \dots, X_p$ is a forest
$\Lambda$ on the planes whose edges carry city labels, such that

* (F1) for every plane $u$ and city $i$, at most $X_u(i)$ edges at $u$ are labelled $i$;
* (F2) $r_u := |X_u| - \deg_\Lambda(u)$ is odd for every plane $u$.

An edge between $u$ and $v$ labelled $i$, a *link* in $i$, is a $(B\bar B)$-pairing; the $r_u$
other landings of $u$, its *free landings*, are performed as patterns $A, \bar A, \dots, A$.
:::

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Lemma 2.6" >}} **Link forest.** A partition is admissible if and only if it has a link
forest.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* Counting the labels of a link forest at each plane gives an integer parity matrix,
which reduces mod 2 to a parity matrix ({{< node "Lemma 2.3" >}}). Conversely, take a parity
matrix supported in a spanning forest of $H$, pair the planes marked in each city, and check
that the pairs form no cycle ({{< node "Lemma 2.6" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

When $|X| = 2t - p$, {{< node "Corollary 2.7" >}} bounds the structure: a link forest has at most
$t - p$ links, and each of its trees has at most $q_{\max} = \min(p, t - p + 1)$ planes.

## Constructing the plan {#sec-achievability}

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Theorem 4.1" >}} Assume (S). For every list $X$ of $2t - p$ cities and every
admissible partition $X_1, \dots, X_p$ of $X$, there is a feasible plan whose central landings are
exactly $X$ (so its cost is $c(X)$), in which plane $k$ flies for $\ell(X_k)$ and performs at most
one pattern $\bar B$, and whose makespan is $\max_k \ell(X_k)$. The plan uses no flight between
central cities.
:::

The construction roots every tree of a link forest at a plane. For a link in $i$ between a parent
$u$ and a child $v$, $u$ performs the pattern $B$ and $v$ the pattern $\bar B$. The western part
of each pairing is performed as early as possible, and its eastern part as late as possible: each
plane flies its patterns $B$ first, from time 0, then its free landings as patterns $A$ and
$\bar A$, then its pattern $\bar B$ if it has a parent. A plane has at most one parent, so it
performs at most one $\bar B$, at the end of its sequence. That $\bar B$ may have to wait for the
passenger, but the parent flies its patterns $B$ first, so the wait ends within the parent's own
duration, and no plane finishes later than its load or its parent's.

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* The child $v$ arrives in $i$ at $\ell(X_v) - d_i$, and the parent's drop-off arrives
there by $\tau_u - d_i$, where $\tau_u \le \ell(X_u)$ is the duration of $u$'s patterns $B$. So
$v$ is back in $C_G$ by $\max(\ell(X_v), \ell(X_u))$, and every plane flies exactly $\ell(X_k)$
({{< node "Theorem 4.1" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

## A lower bound for every plan {#sec-relaxation}

A first lower bound on the cost of every plan comes from forgetting admissibility. It needs a
bound on the duration of a pattern.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Lemma 3.3" >}} **Pattern durations.** Let a pattern $\gamma$ visit the central cities
$x_1, \dots, x_m$ in this order.

*(a)* Under (S), $F(\gamma) \ge d_{x_1} + d_{x_m} \ge 2\min(d_{x_1}, d_{x_m})$.

*(b)* Under (AΔ), for every $j$, $F(\gamma) \ge d_{x_j} + \bar d_{x_j}$ for patterns $A$ and
$\bar A$, $F(\gamma) \ge 2 d_{x_j}$ for $B$ and $F(\gamma) \ge 2\bar d_{x_j}$ for $\bar B$.

*(c)* A simple pattern in $x$ lasts exactly $d_x + \bar d_x$ ($A$, $\bar A$), $2 d_x$ ($B$) or
$2\bar d_x$ ($\bar B$).
:::

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Lemma 3.4" >}} **Relaxation.** Assume (S). For every feasible plan with cost $C$ and
makespan $M$ there are non-empty multisets $Y_1, \dots, Y_p$ with $\sum_k |Y_k| = 2t - p$,
$c(Y_1 + \dots + Y_p) \le C$ and $\ell(Y_k) \le F_k \le M$ for every $k$. Hence, with integer
durations, $C \ge L(\lfloor M/2 \rfloor)$, where
$$L(T) = \min\Big\{c(Y) : Y = Y_1 + \dots + Y_p,\ |Y| = 2t - p,\ Y_k \ne \emptyset \text{ and } \delta(Y_k) \le T \text{ for all } k\Big\}.$$
No assumption on the flights between central cities is needed.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* Charge each pattern to whichever of its first and last central cities has the smaller
$d$, which by Lemma 3.3(a) costs at most half its flight time in load; by Corollary II there are
at least $2t - p$ patterns, at least one per plane, and their charged landings are distinct
({{< node "Lemma 3.4" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

$L$ is the minimisation that defines the front, without admissibility. Wherever it meets the
least cost of an admissible partition, the front is known whatever the flights between central
cities; this is the common case ([certificates](algorithm.qmd#sec-certificates)).

## Proof of Proposition I under the assumption of [QS15] {#sec-converse}

Under (A1), a flight between central cities can always be replaced by a detour through $C_G$:
using the same plane, the passenger on board flies to $C_G$ instead, and the plane flies on to
the next city, arriving no later. The plan then only performs simple patterns, which we read
through the passengers they carry.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Definition 4.2" >}} **Role configuration.** A role configuration assigns to each plane
$k$ three multisets of central cities, its patterns $B$ ($\mathrm{Dr}_k$, drop-offs), $\bar B$
($\mathrm{Pk}_k$, pick-ups) and $A$ or $\bar A$ ($\mathrm{Cr}_k$, crossings), with
$|\mathrm{Cr}_k|$ odd and the *per-city balance* $\sum_k \mathrm{Dr}_k = \sum_k \mathrm{Pk}_k$.
Its passenger count is $\sum_k \big(|\mathrm{Dr}_k| + (|\mathrm{Cr}_k| + 1)/2\big)$, its cost is
$\sum_k c(\mathrm{Dr}_k + \mathrm{Pk}_k + \mathrm{Cr}_k)$, and the *role load* of plane $k$ is
$$\lambda_k = 2\delta(\mathrm{Dr}_k) + 2\bar\delta(\mathrm{Pk}_k) + \delta(\mathrm{Cr}_k) + \bar\delta(\mathrm{Cr}_k).$$
:::

Under (S), $\lambda_k = \ell(X_k)$ for the group $X_k = \mathrm{Dr}_k + \mathrm{Pk}_k + \mathrm{Cr}_k$.
Three lemmas connect plans, role configurations and partitions; call a plan *simple* if all its
patterns are simple.

* {{< node "Lemma 4.3" >}} (direct selection): in a simple plan with clean journeys every journey
  is $C_I \to x \to C_G$, and selecting patterns by their role in the journeys gives a role
  configuration with passenger count at least $t$, cost at most $C$ and $\lambda_k \le F_k$.
* {{< node "Lemma 4.4" >}} (shrinking): deleting two crossings, or a $(B\bar B)$-pairing, brings
  the passenger count down to exactly $t$ without increasing anything.
* {{< node "Lemma 4.5" >}} (parity): the groups of a role configuration with passenger count $t$
  form an admissible partition of $2t - p$ cities, with parity matrix
  $h_{k,i} = (\mathrm{Dr}_k(i) + \mathrm{Pk}_k(i)) \bmod 2$.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Theorem 4.7" >}} **Converse.** Assume (S) and (A1). For every feasible plan with cost
$C$, makespan $M$ and flight times $F_k$, there is an admissible partition $X_1, \dots, X_p$ of a
list $X$ of $2t - p$ cities with $c(X) \le C$ and $\ell(X_k) \le F_k \le M$ for every $k$.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* Replace every flight $a \to b$ between central cities by $a \to C_G \to b$: by (S) and
(A1) the plane reaches $b$ no later, the landings are unchanged, and a passenger on board is
delivered in $C_G$. Then clean the journeys (Lemma 3.1) and apply Lemmas 4.3, 4.4 and 4.5
({{< node "Theorem 4.7" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

With Theorem 4.1 and Lemma 1.1, this proves Proposition I under (A1), in the following precise
form.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Corollary 4.8" >}} Assume (S) and (A1). Then
$$\mathcal F = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal X, \qquad \mathcal X = \{(c(X), M(X)) : |X| = 2t - p,\ M(X) < \infty\},$$
and every point of $\mathcal F$ is attained by a plan with exactly $2t - p$ central landings.
:::

@tbl-example lists an admissible partition for each point of the example instance. Every point
uses two even groups and one $(B\bar B)$-pairing. Groups of sizes 1 and 3 put three landings on
one plane; $\{1\}, \{1, 1, 1\}$ for instance costs 36 with makespan 12, and is dominated by
$(24, 12)$.

| Front point | $X_1$ | $X_2$ | Pairing | Loads |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $(36, 8)$ | $\{1, 1\}$ | $\{1, 1\}$ | in $C_1$ | 8, 8 |
| $(30, 10)$ | $\{1, 2\}$ | $\{1, 2\}$ | in $C_1$ | 10, 10 |
| $(24, 12)$ | $\{2, 2\}$ | $\{2, 2\}$ | in $C_2$ | 12, 12 |
| $(20, 14)$ | $\{1, 3\}$ | $\{1, 3\}$ | in $C_1$ | 14, 14 |

The same holds when planes may finish anywhere, as in PDDL problems without goals on the planes:

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Theorem 4.9" >}} **Bridge.** Assume (S) and (A1). The Pareto front of the variant in
which planes may end anywhere, the makespan being the last arrival of any flight, equals
$\mathcal F$.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* Remove flights between central cities and clean as in Theorem 4.7, delete every flight
after a plane's last flight with a passenger, and complete a sequence that ends with
$C_I \to x$ by $x \to C_G$. The planes left without flights are added back one at a time by
{{< node "Lemma 4.6" >}}, which gives a new plane one city taken from the others without raising
the cost or the largest load ({{< node "Theorem 4.9" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

## Proof of Proposition I under the triangular inequality {#sec-adelta}

Without (A1), the detour through $C_G$ can be longer than the flight it replaces, so a pattern
may visit several central cities while its duration pays for only one of them. Each pattern can
still be *reduced*: by Lemma 3.3(b), under (S) and (AΔ), a pattern lasts at least twice the
duration $d_x$ of every city $x$ it visits, so a simple pattern of the same type in any of these
cities, or in a city of smaller duration, is no longer, and lands only once. Reducing patterns
one by one does not conclude, however. After the reduction, the passenger left by a pattern $B$
may be taken by a pattern $\bar B$ in another city, and moving both to the city of smaller
duration requires two landings there, which may cost more than the two landings they replace.
The proof below does not follow passengers at all.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Theorem 4.10" >}} **Converse without (A1).** Assume (S) and (AΔ). For every feasible
plan with cost $C$, makespan $M$ and flight times $F_k$, there is an admissible partition
$X_1, \dots, X_p$ of a list $X$ of $2t - p$ cities with $c(X) \le C$ and
$\ell(X_k) \le F_k \le M$ for every $k$. The same holds for a plan on any set $Q$ of planes with
$t \ge |Q|$, with $|Q|$ in place of $p$.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* Each pattern is reduced to a city of duration at most the largest $d$ it visits,
provided some landing of the plan pays for it. Planes that share a central city form components,
whose parities Corollary II fixes; $(B\bar B)$-pairings between planes are laid along a spanning
forest of the sharing graph so that every plane gets the right parity, and pairings that meet at
one pattern are re-paired, each moved to the city of smaller duration together with the landing
that pays for it, until every pattern carries at most one. The pairings then define an integer
parity matrix ({{< node "Lemma 2.3" badge=false >}}), and {{< node "Lemma 4.11" >}} removes
landings two at a time down to $2t - p$ ({{< node "Theorem 4.10" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

The proof uses (AΔ) only through the inequality $F(\gamma) \ge 2d_x$ for every central city $x$
of a pattern $\gamma$, which also holds under (A1), so it is a second proof of Theorem 4.7. Under
(S) alone, the same inequality holds with $d_x$ replaced by the shortest flight time $d'_x$ from
$x$ to $C_I$ or $C_G$, so the admissible optimum computed with the durations $d'$ is a lower
bound for every plan, next to $L$. Everything built on Theorem 4.7 carries over:

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Corollary 4.12" >}} Under (S) and (AΔ), Corollary 4.8, Theorem 4.9,
Proposition 7.1, the front statements of Propositions 7.8 and 7.9 hold, and `forest` gaps of a
certificate are sound.
:::

This proves Proposition I under (AΔ). Theorem 4.10 is machine-checked in Lean, as
`Feasible.exists_admissible_ATri`, and so are three parts of Corollary 4.12 that follow from it:
Corollary 4.8 under (AΔ) (`minimal_achievable_iff_multisetPoints_ATri`), and the correctness of
the verified solver and of the certificate checker under (AΔ) (`solveFront_isParetoFront_ATri`,
`Cert.check_sound_ATri`). Independently of the proof, the experiment
[E6](experiments.qmd#sec-e6) searched the gaps where $L$ lies below the admissible optimum, on
small instances with the shortest flights between central cities the triangular inequality
allows, and found no plan cheaper than that optimum.

## The assumption is needed {#sec-ex413}

Without (A1) and (AΔ), a plan can beat every admissible partition, so Proposition I needs some
assumption on the flights between central cities.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Example 4.13" >}} **The hypothesis matters.** Take $d = (2, 3, 9, 11)$,
$c = (50, 44, 17, 0)$, $t = 6$ and $p = 3$, so $2t - p = 9$, and flights between central cities
$d_{12} = 1$, $d_{13} = 5$, $d_{14} = 6$, $d_{23} = 3$, $d_{24} = 6$, $d_{34} = 1$. They satisfy
neither (A1) nor (AΔ): $d_4 = 11 > d_{34} + d_3 = 10$. The front of admissible partitions has the
consecutive points $(264, 34)$ and $(228, 40)$, so every admissible partition with makespan below
40 costs at least 264. A plan has makespan 39 and cost $260 = L(19)$.
:::

In that plan, one plane performs the pattern $C_I \to C_4 \to C_3 \to C_I$: it leaves a passenger
in $C_4$ at time 11 and comes back through $C_3$, in $1 + 9 < d_4$, so its pattern lasts
$21 < 2 d_4$. The plan was found with an integer flow model, simulated, and confirmed with a second
solver (computed). Under (S) alone, the exact front is open; $L$ and the admissible optimum with
the durations $d'$ remain lower bounds.

In conclusion, we proved that for the Symmetric MultiZenoTravel problem, under the triangular
inequality as well as under the assumption of [[QS15](index.qmd#ref-QS15)], every point of the
Pareto front is attained by a plan using exactly $2t - p$ central cities, flown without waiting
from an admissible partition. This will allow a constructive algorithm to drastically reduce the
search space of feasible and Pareto-optimal plans ([Pareto Optimal Plans](algorithm.qmd)).
